summary: West Bend Insurance's safety blog post 'Property Damage from Rain Water' opens with a 'Reality Alert' about a preschool whose basement flooded during a weekend thunderstorm after a sump pump failed during a power outage. It presents water damage statistics and then lists common rain-water problem sources: parking lots, ground pitch, gutters, downspouts, and sump pumps, each with loss prevention tips. Site navigation, footers, and tracking boilerplate were ignored.
one_line: West Bend Insurance safety blog on preventing rain-water property damage, covering a preschool flood case, water damage statistics, and maintenance tips for parking lots, gutters, downspouts and sump pumps.
key_facts: A weekend thunderstorm at a preschool resulted in over $15,000 in damages to personal property within the building and over $20,000 to the building itself.
Water began to fill the basin beneath the preschool building's basement after heavy rains.
The preschool's basement sump pump failed to engage because the power went out.
The note says a back up generator for the sump pump would have worked regardless of the power outage.
Water damage is the second most frequently filed insurance claim in the United States.
Water damage claims account for $11 billion dollars in damages annually.
The average cost of a water damage claim is $5,000.
Up to 93% of the cost of water damage could have been prevented by the use of a shut-off system or water leak detection system.
8% of all water damage to buildings is due to weather.
Parking lots are designed to deliver runoff water to a drainage system, but leaf litter, debris, ice, and garbage can clog drains.
Snow piles should not be placed over storm drains or directly next to the building.
Standing water in a parking lot is a tell-tale sign that water is not draining properly.
If the ground is pitched toward the building, water will run back toward the building causing leaks and damage.
Gutters should be routinely inspected and cleaned, since a clogged downspout causes overflow.
If water collects at the end of a downspout, an extender can be added or a trench dug to run water away from the building.
Sump pumps act as a last line of defense against water seeping into a facility's basement.
It is recommended to equip a sump pump with a back up generator that will kick in should the facility lose power.
